tagline: Built for pleasant transit, no two bridges alike.
intro: Route 15 crosses into Connecticut at Greenwich and runs 37 miles through the woods of Fairfield County to the Housatonic River at Stratford, two lanes each way and no trucks. It went in between 1934 and 1940 to ease the Boston Post Road, and planners met bitter local opposition by calling in landscape architects. The Merritt Parkway Conservancy's page still quotes Congressman Schuyler Merritt, who said the road was "not being constructed primarily for rapid transit but for pleasant transit."

George Dunkelberger designed all 69 bridges, each decorated so that no two looked alike, in a range of styles, Art Deco and Art Moderne most notably. Some entrances still have stop signs and no merge lane at all.

moments.title: Silvermine
moments.text: An art colony along the Silvermine River, which once turned a dozen mills, keeps a name from legends of a silver mine. No silver has ever been found.

moments.title: The No Exit Zone
moments.text: Between Westport and Fairfield the parkway runs about five and a half miles without an exit, a stretch the traffic reports call No Man's Land.

moments.title: Boothe Memorial Park, Stratford
moments.text: Near the end a park of odd buildings, among them a windmill and a miniature lighthouse, keeps the last highway toll booth in Connecticut, log-built and retired in 1988.

practical: Trucks, buses, trailers and towed vehicles, and anything 8 feet tall or taller, are barred from the whole parkway because of its low bridges, narrow lanes and tight curves.

sources.label: Wikipedia, Boothe Memorial Park and Museum
